grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('vakatungamirira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vakatungamirira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('kuvachena')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'kuvachena'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('yavo')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'yavo' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: Mbuya Nehanda (Charwe Nyakasikana) & the First Chimurenga (1896–1897)
cultural_notes.content: Nyakasikana, revered as the medium of the ancestral spirit Nehanda ('Mbuya Nehanda'), was one of the foremost spiritual and resistance leaders of the First Chimurenga (1896–1897) in Mashonaland, inspiring generations in the struggle for land and self-determination.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this sentence using the Present Progressive ('is reading right now'): 'Shamwari yangu ______ bhuku idzva.'
active_exercises.explanation: 'Shamwari' uses the progressive form 'iri ku-' + '-verenga' (read) to mean 'is reading right now'.

active_exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'Mbuya vari kurima' instead of 'Mbuya ari kurima' when talking about one grandmother?
options: Because 'mbuya' always refers to three or more people
Because 'vari' is only used for the future tense
Because 'ari' can only be used with inanimate objects
Shona uses the plural prefix 'va-' ('vari') to show polite respect to elders and parents
active_exercises.correct_answer: Shona uses the plural prefix 'va-' ('vari') to show polite respect to elders and parents
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, respected family elders ('amai', 'baba', 'mbuya', 'sekuru') always take the polite plural 'va-' agreement.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this new sentence in the past tense: 'Nezuro amai ______ sadza nenyama.' (Yesterday Mother cooked sadza and meat.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Amai' takes the respectful plural past prefix 'vaka-' + '-bika' (cook) -> 'vakabika' ('cooked').
